skills.name: Prepare hydrogen sulphide in the laboratory and state its physical properties

note.text:
Laboratory preparation: a metal sulphide and a dilute acid.
FeS + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2S
Iron(II) sulphide is placed in a flask and dilute hydrochloric acid is run onto it. No heat is needed. The gas is collected by downward delivery, because it is denser than air.
Dilute sulphuric acid may be used instead. Nitric acid must not be used: it is an oxidising acid and gives sulphur instead.
Physical properties: a colourless, very poisonous gas smelling of rotten eggs; denser than air (relative molecular mass 34); fairly soluble in water, giving a weakly acidic solution. It dulls the sense of smell, so it must always be made in a fume cupboard.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to write the equation for preparing hydrogen sulphide, explain how it is collected and state its properties and dangers.
Builds on: Lesson {3} (preparing a gas and collecting it) and Form Three acids with salts.
Leads to: Lesson {6} (the chemical properties of {formula('H2S')}) and the sulphides of Lesson {7}.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.text:
A metal sulphide and a dilute acid give hydrogen sulphide:
{formula('FeS')} + {2}{formula('HCl')} → {formula('FeCl2')} + {formula('H2S')}
Lumps of iron(II) sulphide are placed in a flask and dilute hydrochloric acid is run onto them from a thistle funnel. No heating is needed.
Dilute sulphuric acid works as well. Nitric acid must NOT be used: it is an oxidising acid and would oxidise the hydrogen sulphide to sulphur, leaving a yellow deposit instead of a gas.

sections.heading: Physical properties and safety
sections.text:
Hydrogen sulphide is a colourless gas with the smell of rotten eggs.
Its relative molecular mass is {2} × {1} + {32} = {34}, above the average for air, so it is denser than air and is collected by downward delivery.
It is fairly soluble in water, giving a weakly acidic solution that turns blue litmus red.
It is very poisonous. Worse, it quickly dulls the sense of smell, so a worker may stop noticing it while still breathing it in. It must always be prepared and used in a fume cupboard.

key_words.meaning: a compound of a metal with sulphur, such as {formula('FeS')}
an acid such as nitric acid that oxidises what it reacts with
collecting a dense gas at the bottom of a jar

mistake.wrong: hydrogen sulphide is prepared with dilute nitric acid
mistake.right: a non-oxidising acid such as hydrochloric acid is used
mistake.why: Nitric acid would oxidise the gas to sulphur, so none would be collected.

worked_example.problem: Write the equation for the laboratory preparation of hydrogen sulphide and explain why nitric acid is not used.
steps: A metal sulphide with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen sulphide.
Nitric acid is an oxidising acid.
It would oxidise the hydrogen sulphide to sulphur, so the gas would not be collected.
worked_example.answer: {formula('FeS')} + {2}{formula('HCl')} → {formula('FeCl2')} + {formula('H2S')}; nitric acid would oxidise the gas to sulphur

pick.q: Which reagents are used to prepare hydrogen sulphide in the laboratory?
pick.r: Iron(II) sulphide and dilute hydrochloric acid
w: Iron(II) sulphate and dilute hydrochloric acid
Iron filings and dilute hydrochloric acid
Iron(II) sulphide and concentrated nitric acid
e: A sulphate gives no {formula('H2S')} with a dilute acid; a sulphide does.
Iron with a dilute acid gives hydrogen, not hydrogen sulphide.
Concentrated nitric acid is an oxidising acid; it would oxidise the sulphide to sulphur.

pick.q: What does hydrogen sulphide smell like?
e: The sharp choking smell is sulphur dioxide.
Even a trace can be smelt, which is one way it is noticed.
pick.y: {formula('H2S')} is a colourless, poisonous gas that smells of rotten eggs.

pick.r: By downward delivery, because it is denser than air
w: Over water in an open trough
e: Its relative molecular mass is {34}, above the average for air, so it sinks.
It is fairly soluble in water, so some would be lost.
It is collected in the ordinary way, in a fume cupboard.
pick.y: A gas denser than air and soluble in water is collected by downward delivery.

pick.q: Why is hydrogen sulphide dangerous to work with?
pick.r: It is very poisonous, and it dulls the sense of smell so that it may not be noticed
w: It explodes in contact with air
It is only unpleasant, not harmful
It burns the skin on contact
e: It burns in air, but it does not explode on contact.
It is seriously poisonous and has killed people.
The danger is from breathing it in, not from skin contact.
pick.y: After a short time the smell can no longer be noticed, so the gas must always be used in a fume cupboard.

pick.q: How does hydrogen sulphide behave in water?
pick.r: It dissolves fairly well, giving a weakly acidic solution
w: It dissolves to give an alkaline solution
e: It is fairly soluble: a few volumes dissolve in one volume of water.
The solution turns blue litmus red, so it is acidic.
There is no violent reaction; it simply dissolves.
pick.y: The solution is a weak acid, sometimes called hydrosulphuric acid.

questions.prompt: Find the relative molecular mass of {formula(F)}.

misconceptions.explain: {totalAtoms(F)} is the number of atoms, not the mass.
Include every atom in the formula, not just the first element.

solution: Add the relative atomic mass of every atom in the formula.
The relative molecular mass of {formula(F)} is {answer}.

questions.prompt: Why must hydrogen sulphide always be prepared in a fume cupboard?
What volume of hydrogen sulphide, in dm³ at s.t.p., is given off when {n} mol of iron(II) sulphide reacts completely with dilute hydrochloric acid?

misconceptions.explain: The equation gives {1} mol of gas for each {1} mol of sulphide, not {2}.

solution: At s.t.p. {1} mol of any gas is {22.4} dm³, so the volume is {n} × {22.4} = {answer} dm³.

questions.prompt: What mass of iron(II) sulphide, in grams, is needed to make {n} mol of hydrogen sulphide?

misconceptions.explain: Mass = moles × molar mass: multiply, do not divide.
The question asks for the mass of {formula('FeS')}, not of the gas.

solution: {1} mol of {formula('FeS')} gives {1} mol of {formula('H2S')}, so {n} mol of {formula('FeS')} is needed.
The relative formula mass of {formula('FeS')} is {molarMass('FeS')}.
